title: Market making
text: A market maker shows a price to buy and a price to sell, all day long. It earns the gap between them, and it is paid for carrying risk that others do not want. Here is how that works, and how it goes wrong.

title: The round trip
text: Picture a stock quoted at 100.00 bid and 100.02 offered. The maker joins both sides with 100 shares each. A buyer lifts the offer, so the maker sells at 100.02. Later a seller hits the bid, so it buys back at 100.00. It is flat again, two cents a share richer. That round trip is the edge, and it is tiny, so the business only works at very high volume.

title: How it loses
text: There are two ways to lose. Inventory risk: after one fill, the price can drift before the other side ever trades. Adverse selection: the trader who hits you may know something you do not. Those fills arrive just before the price moves against you. Glosten and Milgrom showed in 1985 that part of every spread is the price of trading with better-informed traders.

title: Avellaneda-Stoikov
text: Avellaneda and Stoikov made this precise in 2008. First, the maker moves its own fair value, the reservation price, away from the mid. The shift is inventory, times risk aversion, times variance, times the time left. Being long lowers both quotes, so a sale becomes likelier than another purchase. Then it sets a spread around that price. One part pays for risk, the other depends on how fast fills dry up as quotes move away. With the paper's own example values, the total spread comes to about 1.69. Holding two units long moves the reservation price from 100 down to 99.2.

title: In the lab
text: The lab's market maker is a simpler cousin. It joins the best bid and offer, or steps one tick inside when the spread is three ticks or wider. It leans both quotes one tick for every 100 shares it holds, and stops quoting a side at 1,000 shares. It leaves an order alone within one tick, because a replace loses queue position. Replayed on one day of real Nasdaq data, Apple on January 30, 2019, it lost about 20 thousand dollars over 33 thousand fills.

title: What it needs
text: So the quoting rule is the easy part. Professionals add colocated servers and direct feeds, so quotes react within microseconds. Fast cancels matter, because a stale quote is a free option for someone faster. Short-term signals, like the microprice, let a maker lean before the move. And hard limits on inventory and loss, with a kill switch, cap the bad days.

title: Takeaway
text: Market making harvests the spread, and pays for it in inventory risk and adverse selection. Speed, signals and risk limits decide who gets to keep it.
